source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3

coverage.syllabusClasses: Classes 8–12 (Sep. 21, 23, 28, 30; Oct. 5), first part of adjudication unit

topics.title: § 3.1 / 3.1.1 — Federal Statutory Hearing Rights (pp. 77–85)
topics.description: Classes 8–9 · Type A/B/C; APA § 554(a) gateway; Union Pacific; statutory-versus-constitutional requirements.

entries.title: Start with the source of the claimed hearing right
entries.summary: Constitutional due process and agency-specific statutes independently create hearing rights; both may apply, neither may apply, or only one may apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: A constitutionally fair hearing is not automatically an APA trial; a statute may require more formality than the Constitution.
entries.legalExplanation: First analyze constitutional due process (Chapter 2) and statutory procedures separately. The federal APA supplies Type A procedures only when its gateway is opened; state APAs vary.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 77–78
entries.examApplication: Identify government action, due process threshold, statute requiring hearing, APA gateway, and governing procedures in that sequence.
entries.examTrap: A due process hearing does not automatically become a Type A proceeding.

entries.title: Three categories: Type A, Type B, and Type C
entries.summary: Type A = APA adjudication under §§ 554, 556, 557; Type B = statutorily required evidentiary hearing not governed by APA formal-hearing provisions; Type C = no statutory evidentiary hearing mandate.
entries.laymanExplanation: A is an APA trial, B is a non-APA evidence-based trial, and C is a flexible administrative decision process.
entries.legalExplanation: A and B both rely on evidence as the exclusive basis for decision, but Type A brings APA ALJ and procedural safeguards. Type C typically includes letters, meetings, or negotiations and is largely agency-designed; APA §§ 555 and 558 still matter.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 77–79
entries.elements: Type A: APA gateway opened. Type B: hearing required, but not Type A. Type C: no statute requires an evidentiary hearing.
entries.examTrap: Do not equate Type B with casual or non-evidentiary proceedings; it can be highly formal.

entries.title: The APA § 554(a) gateway
entries.summary: A federal adjudication enters Type A procedures when another statute requires it to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing, subject to § 554(a) exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Find a separate statute that calls for an adjudicatory hearing, then ask whether Congress meant a formal APA proceeding.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 554(a) does not itself create general entitlement to a hearing. Distinguish an adjudicatory proceeding from rulemaking, then interpret the governing statute's demand for an on-the-record hearing.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 78–80
entries.rule: 5 U.S.C. § 554(a): adjudication required by statute to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.
entries.elements: (1) Adjudication; (2) external statutory hearing requirement; (3) statutory intent to trigger an on-the-record adjudication; (4) no applicable § 554(a) exception.
entries.examTrap: Do not mechanically require the exact words 'on the record' in every circuit.

entries.title: What changes when Type A applies
entries.summary: Type A ordinarily uses protected ALJs, separates adversary and deciding functions, bars merits-related ex parte communications, permits necessary cross-examination, and assigns the proponent burden of proof.
entries.laymanExplanation: Formal APA adjudication comes with a more protected judge and stronger fairness safeguards.
entries.legalExplanation: §§ 554(d), 556(d), 557(d) govern separation, evidentiary presentation/cross-examination, and ex parte contacts. EAJA attorney-fee rules may apply to qualifying Type A adjudications but not to Types B/C.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 78–79
entries.elements: ALJ or statute-authorized presiding official; separation of functions; ex parte restrictions; cross-examination needed for full disclosure; burden on order proponent; potential EAJA fees.
entries.examTrap: The text distinguishes ALJs from AJs (e.g., immigration judges), who do not enjoy identical APA safeguards.

entries.title: Meaning of 'on the record' and conflicting gateway tests
entries.summary: Some courts demand clear or express statutory 'on the record' language; others use congressional intent and adjudication's quasi-judicial character even without magic words.
entries.laymanExplanation: 'Hearing' alone might or might not trigger the formal APA system depending on the statute and controlling precedent.
entries.legalExplanation: For exclusive-record adjudication the decision normally rests only on evidence properly introduced at hearing (§ 556(e)). Type B also has an exclusive record, so the phrase is a congressional-intent signal, not proof of a transcript.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 79–83
entries.examApplication: Quote the actual statute ('public hearing,' 'full hearing,' or 'hearing on the record') and compare circuit approaches.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse a stenographic transcript with an exclusive evidentiary decision record.

entries.title: Union Pacific Railroad Co. v. Surface Transportation Board, 113 F.4th 823 (8th Cir. 2024)
entries.summary: Yes. The Eighth Circuit held that the full-hearing statute triggers Type A adjudication despite absence of magic words; FORR could not be used to set rates under that process, and the order was vacated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Simply: Yes. The Eighth Circuit held that the full-hearing statute triggers Type A adjudication despite absence of magic words; FORR could not be used to set rates under that process, and the order was vacated.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Did the 'full hearing' requirement trigger APA § 554(a), rendering FORR incompatible with statutory APA adjudication rules? Reasoning: Congress clearly contemplated quasi-judicial hearings; magic words were not indispensable. The court used independent statutory judgment after Loper Bright, and FORR's either-or constraint conflicted with APA burden-of-proof requirements.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 80–81
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied reading
entries.facts: STB created Final Offer Rate Review (FORR), requiring the Board to select a railroad's or a shipper's last proposed rate. Congress demanded a 'full hearing' for rate reasonableness disputes, without the literal words 'on the record'.
entries.issue: Did the 'full hearing' requirement trigger APA § 554(a), rendering FORR incompatible with statutory APA adjudication rules?
entries.holding: Yes. The Eighth Circuit held that the full-hearing statute triggers Type A adjudication despite absence of magic words; FORR could not be used to set rates under that process, and the order was vacated.
entries.reasoning: Congress clearly contemplated quasi-judicial hearings; magic words were not indispensable. The court used independent statutory judgment after Loper Bright, and FORR's either-or constraint conflicted with APA burden-of-proof requirements.
entries.rule: Section 554(a) can be triggered by clear statutory intent for a formal adjudicatory hearing without express 'on the record' words (Eighth Circuit reading).
entries.examApplication: Analyze hearing terminology, whether adjudication is involved, burdens of proof, and effects of Loper Bright on agency interpretive claims.
entries.examTrap: Do not universalize Union Pacific as a Supreme Court resolution of every circuit's contested gateway approach.

entries.title: City of West Chicago v. NRC, 701 F.2d 632 (7th Cir. 1983)
entries.summary: Illustrates the restrictive 'magic words' approach.
entries.laymanExplanation: Illustrates the restrictive 'magic words' approach.
entries.legalExplanation: Treated express 'on the record' language or equivalent strong signals as necessary to open the APA gateway.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 79–82
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Contrast with Union Pacific and Seacoast.

entries.title: Seacoast Anti-Pollution League v. Costle, 572 F.2d 872 (1st Cir. 1978)
entries.summary: Read a statutory 'public hearing' in water permitting as calling for APA Type A procedures.
entries.laymanExplanation: Read a statutory 'public hearing' in water permitting as calling for APA Type A procedures.
entries.legalExplanation: Rejected the magic-words restriction in its context; later overruled in the First Circuit by Chevron-based Dominion.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 81–82
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Compare agency interpretation and statutory judicial judgment before/after Loper Bright.

entries.title: Dominion Energy Brayton Point v. Johnson, 443 F.3d 12 (1st Cir. 2006)
entries.summary: Relied on Chevron to accept an agency's reasonable interpretation that a statutory hearing need not require Type A.
entries.laymanExplanation: Relied on Chevron to accept an agency's reasonable interpretation that a statutory hearing need not require Type A.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook emphasizes that Chevron was overruled in Loper Bright, while Loper Bright cautioned against automatic repudiation of settled holdings relying on Chevron.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 81–83
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Flag potential precedent tension; do not claim Dominion was overruled solely because Chevron was.

entries.title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)
entries.summary: Courts exercise independent judgment about statutory meaning; Chevron deference was overruled.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts exercise independent judgment about statutory meaning; Chevron deference was overruled.
entries.legalExplanation: Pre-Chevron agency interpretations no longer control by reason of ambiguity alone; the Court preserved ordinary statutory stare decisis for earlier statutory holdings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 80–83
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Explain why Union Pacific invoked Loper Bright but did not reconcile Dominion.

entries.title: Type B fairness and limits of court-created procedures
entries.summary: Even if statutory hearing does not open the APA gateway, agency statutes and regulations may protect impartiality and cross-examination; courts are constrained in imposing procedures beyond statute and due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency's non-APA hearing still must obey applicable rules, but judges cannot freely rewrite its procedure.
entries.legalExplanation: United States Lines and Finer Foods construed hearing language to imply basic safeguards; Vermont Yankee and PBGC limit court-imposed additional procedural requirements beyond applicable law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 83–84
entries.examApplication: Check the particular statute, procedural regulations, constitutional floor, and any controlling interpretation; do not import all Type A requirements by instinct.
entries.examTrap: The textbook calls certain pre-PBGC judicial innovations questionable, not necessarily categorically overruled.

entries.title: United States Lines, Inc. v. FMC, 584 F.2d 519 (D.C. Cir. 1978)
entries.summary: Interpreted 'notice and hearing' to require protection against merits-related ex parte contacts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Interpreted 'notice and hearing' to require protection against merits-related ex parte contacts.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook offers it as judicial protection in non-Type A hearings, but notes later doubts under Vermont Yankee and PBGC.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 83
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Use as contested authority, not a universal statutory ban.

entries.title: Finer Foods, Inc. v. USDA, 274 F.3d 1137 (7th Cir. 2001)
entries.summary: Treated a hearing-before-license-suspension requirement as demanding a neutral decisionmaker.
entries.laymanExplanation: Treated a hearing-before-license-suspension requirement as demanding a neutral decisionmaker.
entries.legalExplanation: Again, textbook flags doctrinal tension with constraints on judicially added procedures.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 83
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Test for independent statutory basis or due process.

entries.title: PBGC v. LTV Corp., 496 U.S. 633 (1990)
entries.summary: Extended Vermont Yankee procedural-restraint reasoning to adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: Extended Vermont Yankee procedural-restraint reasoning to adjudication.
entries.legalExplanation: Without additional statutory or constitutional command, the agency generally chooses its own adjudication procedures, subject to APA minima.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 83–84
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Contrast §§ 555, 558 with full Type A safeguards.

entries.title: ACUS best practices for Type B adjudication
entries.summary: ACUS Recommendation 2016-4 favors notice, prohibition of improper ex parte contacts, appropriate cross-examination, and reasoned written decisions through agency regulations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Type B hearings can be made fair by agency-written rules, even without the full APA.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency regulations can adopt Type A-like safeguards voluntarily; ABA's 2000 proposal to make every new statutory 'hearing' presumptively Type A had not been enacted according to the textbook.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 84
entries.examTrap: Recommendations are not mandatory statutory law.

entries.title: Wong Yang Sung v. McGrath, 339 U.S. 33 (1950)
entries.summary: Held due-process-required deportation hearings could trigger APA § 554(a) even without a hearing statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Held due-process-required deportation hearings could trigger APA § 554(a) even without a hearing statute.
entries.legalExplanation: Congress promptly displaced the immigration-specific result; the broader constitutional-hearing gateway theory is largely ignored or avoided in later lower-court decisions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 84–85
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Treat Wong as a contested residual doctrine, not present-day immigration APA coverage.

topics.title: § 3.1.2 — State Statutory Hearing Rights (pp. 85–91)
topics.description: Classes 9–10 · 1961/1981 Model State APA approaches; Oregon; Florida; Metsch; Ralph problem.

entries.title: Compare state APA gateway models
entries.summary: 1961 MSAPA: external law must require a hearing; 1981 MSAPA: broadly inclusive adjudication definition; Oregon: a hybrid including constitutional/regulatory triggers and discretionary rights/license revocations; Florida: hearings when substantial interests determined.
entries.laymanExplanation: States do not all follow federal APA § 554(a).
entries.legalExplanation: Identify the state law version before determining whether a contested case requires a hearing. 'Required by law' may include due process and rules under some states' 1961-model interpretation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 85–86
entries.elements: 1961 external-source; 1981 inclusive; Oregon hybrid; Florida substantial interests.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all 'contested cases' hinge on 'hearing on the record' or that constitutional entitlement and statutory substantial interest are identical.

entries.title: 1961 Model State APA — definition of contested case
entries.summary: A contested case is a proceeding where a party's legal rights, duties or privileges are required by law to be determined after an opportunity for hearing.
entries.laymanExplanation: If another law demands a hearing, the state's APA rules follow.
entries.legalExplanation: The scope of 'law' is contested but most referenced cases include hearings required by constitutions and agency regulations, not only statutes.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 85–86
entries.examApplication: Find what law requires a hearing before invoking contested-case provisions.

entries.title: Oregon hybrid and student discipline
entries.summary: Oregon extends contested-case procedures to certain revocation, suspension, or refusal of rights, privileges or licenses, even where no external hearing is otherwise mandated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Oregon may provide an administrative trial where the Constitution would demand less.
entries.legalExplanation: Liu applied formal APA protections to student disciplinary expulsion; Morrison involved clinical-performance dismissal. The textbook questions whether such proceedings are too elaborate.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 86
entries.examTrap: Distinguish full Oregon procedural entitlements from minimal due process in Goss/academic-dismissal settings.

entries.title: Metsch v. University of Florida, 550 So. 2d 1149 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 1989)
entries.summary: No. A sincere wish to enter the university was a unilateral expectation, not a substantial interest requiring a formal hearing; denial affirmed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Simply: No. A sincere wish to enter the university was a unilateral expectation, not a substantial interest requiring a formal hearing; denial affirmed.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Did denial of admission determine the applicant's 'substantial interests' within Florida APA § 120.57(1)? Reasoning: The court demanded immediate injury-in-fact of the type the statutory proceeding is designed to protect. A bare educational aspiration did not suffice; judges also worried about hearings for every rejected applicant.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 86–88
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied reading
entries.facts: Rejected Florida law school applicant sought a formal administrative hearing after denial, alleging a substantial interest merely in attending the school and becoming a lawyer.
entries.issue: Did denial of admission determine the applicant's 'substantial interests' within Florida APA § 120.57(1)?
entries.holding: No. A sincere wish to enter the university was a unilateral expectation, not a substantial interest requiring a formal hearing; denial affirmed.
entries.reasoning: The court demanded immediate injury-in-fact of the type the statutory proceeding is designed to protect. A bare educational aspiration did not suffice; judges also worried about hearings for every rejected applicant.
entries.rule: Under the Metsch construction, Florida's 'substantial interests' gateway requires sufficiently immediate injury-in-fact within the relevant statute's protective scope.
entries.examApplication: Separate inclusive statutory substantial-interest tests from Roth's constitutionally protected property interest, and ask whether disputed material facts warrant formal or informal procedures.
entries.examTrap: The authors criticize importing due-process/property and judicial-standing concepts into an independent statutory standard; their critique is not the court's holding.

entries.title: Liu v. Portland State University, 383 P.3d 294 (Or. Ct. App. 2016)
entries.summary: Oregon's contested-case protections applied to disciplinary student expulsion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Oregon's contested-case protections applied to disciplinary student expulsion.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook lists counsel, confrontation/cross-examination, subpoena and oath protections as examples of Oregon's formal procedures.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 86
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Contrast constitutional minima in Goss and academic dismissals.

entries.title: Morrison v. University of Oregon Health Sciences Center, 685 P.2d 439 (Or. Ct. App. 1984)
entries.summary: Oregon contested-case procedures applied to dental student's dismissal for clinical performance.
entries.laymanExplanation: Oregon contested-case procedures applied to dental student's dismissal for clinical performance.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory right can exceed the constitutional procedural floor for academic decisions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 86
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Show external statutory gateway may be broader than Roth/Mathews.

entries.title: School Board of Palm Beach County v. Survivors Charter Schools, Inc., 3 So. 3d 1220 (Fla. 2009)
entries.summary: Applied the two-part 'substantial interests' test but found the charter-school statute displaced APA procedure.
entries.laymanExplanation: Applied the two-part 'substantial interests' test but found the charter-school statute displaced APA procedure.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook warns that substantial-interest analysis resembles standing but addresses a distinct procedural question.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 89
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Analyze statutory preemption even when a substantial interest exists.

entries.title: Florida informal proceedings where no disputed material fact
entries.summary: If no disputed issue of material fact exists, Florida § 120.57(2) permits informal proceedings: notice and grounds, opportunity to challenge orally or in writing, and written response if rejected.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not every substantial-interest case requires a full trial.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook lists simple procedural steps and asks whether Metsch's admissions dispute had a genuinely contested material fact.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 89–90
entries.elements: Written notice/grounds; oral or written objection opportunity; written denial explanation within seven days if objections rejected.
entries.examTrap: A disputed legal/policy disagreement is not necessarily a disputed material fact.

topics.title: § 3.2 — Rules Limiting Hearing Issues (pp. 91–98)
topics.description: Classes 9–10 · Heckler's grid, rulemaking versus official notice, waivers, administrative summary judgment.

entries.title: General factual rules may resolve issues without individual hearing testimony
entries.summary: Even if statute promises an individualized hearing, the agency can settle certain general facts by valid rule and reserve truly individualized factual disputes for hearings.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can challenge your personal facts at a hearing, but the agency need not re-prove nationwide general facts in every case.
entries.legalExplanation: A promulgated general rule applies conclusively to issues within its scope absent statutory contrary intent or an applicable exception. The casebook contrasts legislative facts with individualized historical facts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 91–95
entries.examApplication: Divide the disputed facts into individual claimant circumstances and facts capable of general regulatory resolution.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse binding rules with rebuttable official notice.

entries.title: Heckler v. Campbell, 461 U.S. 458 (1983)
entries.summary: Yes. SSA could validly resolve general national-job-availability facts by rulemaking while individually determining each claimant's characteristics; the Second Circuit was reversed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Simply: Yes. SSA could validly resolve general national-job-availability facts by rulemaking while individually determining each claimant's characteristics; the Second Circuit was reversed.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Can SSA use generally adopted medical-vocational guidelines instead of vocational-expert proof of available jobs in each disability hearing? Reasoning: Statutory individualized disability hearing requirements do not bar rules settling recurring, general issues. Rulemaking provides fairness and uniformity for national labor market facts, while claimants may present evidence about their abilities and whether the grid fits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 91–95
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied reading
entries.facts: SSA denied Carmen Campbell disability benefits using a medical-vocational grid based on exertional capacity, age, education and work experience. The lower appellate court insisted on individualized identification of available jobs.
entries.issue: Can SSA use generally adopted medical-vocational guidelines instead of vocational-expert proof of available jobs in each disability hearing?
entries.holding: Yes. SSA could validly resolve general national-job-availability facts by rulemaking while individually determining each claimant's characteristics; the Second Circuit was reversed.
entries.reasoning: Statutory individualized disability hearing requirements do not bar rules settling recurring, general issues. Rulemaking provides fairness and uniformity for national labor market facts, while claimants may present evidence about their abilities and whether the grid fits.
entries.rule: An agency may decide general classes of facts by rulemaking despite hearing statutes unless Congress clearly directs otherwise; individualized material facts still require case-specific determinations.
entries.examApplication: Separate grid's general vocational facts from claimant-specific medical and functional facts; argue nonapplication if atypical limitations arise.
entries.examTrap: The holding does not permit the agency to disregard individual limitations or to use 'official notice' as a conclusive, nonrebuttable rule.

entries.title: Binding rules versus rebuttable official notice
entries.summary: A valid general regulation resolves the covered issue conclusively, whereas agency official notice of an adjudicative fact must permit rebuttal under § 556(e).
entries.laymanExplanation: Rule = normally binding. Official notice = someone can challenge the noticed fact.
entries.legalExplanation: Heckler notes that public rulemaking already provides process for testing facts generalized in regulations; official notice in an individual case demands adequate response rights.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 94–95
entries.examTrap: Official notice and legislative rulemaking are different procedural devices.

entries.title: American Hospital Association v. NLRB, 499 U.S. 606 (1991)
entries.summary: General bargaining-unit rules may displace per-case determinations unless Congress clearly withholds that power.
entries.laymanExplanation: General bargaining-unit rules may displace per-case determinations unless Congress clearly withholds that power.
entries.legalExplanation: Extended Heckler's rulemaking-in-adjudication principle in collective-bargaining unit contexts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 95–96
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Explain a presumption of agency rulemaking authority on generalized issues.

entries.title: United States v. Storer Broadcasting Co., 351 U.S. 192 (1956)
entries.summary: Recognized rules resolving classes of recurring issues despite otherwise required adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: Recognized rules resolving classes of recurring issues despite otherwise required adjudication.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook discusses potential exceptions/waivers (safety valves) as a mitigating feature.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 94–96
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Use to discuss flexibility and individual exceptions.

entries.title: FPC v. Texaco Inc., 377 U.S. 33 (1964)
entries.summary: Reinforced ability to employ policy rules despite individualized-hearing schemes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Reinforced ability to employ policy rules despite individualized-hearing schemes.
entries.legalExplanation: Along with Storer, supports Heckler; waiver was relevant but not universally required.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 94–96
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Distinguish factual validity of the rule from right to exceptions.

entries.title: Safety valves, waivers, and atypical claimants
entries.summary: An express waiver is not necessarily a prerequisite to valid adjudication-trumping regulations; some rules protect atypical claimants by declaring themselves inapplicable to unmatched facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rules can make thousands of cases faster but must not be mechanically applied to people they do not cover.
entries.legalExplanation: Heckler's grid excludes significant non-exertional limitations such as pain or psychological conditions from mechanical treatment; a rule's own scope can be a safeguard even without waiver petition rights.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 96–97
entries.examApplication: Ask first whether client's facts fit the rule, then whether rule creates exceptions or waiver procedures, then whether validity itself can be challenged.

entries.title: FCC v. WNCN Listeners Guild, 450 U.S. 582 (1981)
entries.summary: FCC could categorically exclude programming-format changes from broadcast-renewal review.
entries.laymanExplanation: FCC could categorically exclude programming-format changes from broadcast-renewal review.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook uses dissent's waiver concern to show categorical rules need not automatically include exceptions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 96
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Discuss tradeoff between efficiency and individualized equity.

entries.title: Yetman v. Garvey, 261 F.3d 664 (7th Cir. 2001)
entries.summary: Illustrates FAA categorical airline pilot retirement policy and resistance to individual waivers.
entries.laymanExplanation: Illustrates FAA categorical airline pilot retirement policy and resistance to individual waivers.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency feared case-by-case medical examinations would defeat the uniform rule's purpose.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 96–97
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Discuss costs of discretionary exceptions.

entries.title: Administrative summary judgment and useless hearings
entries.summary: A statutory hearing can be denied when no genuine material factual dispute requires live evidence; agencies may employ summary-judgment-like procedures.
entries.laymanExplanation: No trial is necessary just to argue something that cannot affect the outcome.
entries.legalExplanation: Weinberger v. Hynson approved a regulatory threshold for hearings before FDA drug-license withdrawals; the casebook also discusses FERC denial where disagreement concerned policy rather than historical facts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 97–98
entries.elements: Identify governing rule; material factual issue; admissible evidence supporting dispute; whether testimony could contribute to fair resolution.
entries.examTrap: A claimant's demand for 'a hearing' does not eliminate the need to proffer a genuine material factual dispute.

entries.title: Weinberger v. Hynson, Westcott & Dunning, Inc., 412 U.S. 609 (1973)
entries.summary: FDA may withhold hearing when proffer raises no genuine and substantial factual issue.
entries.laymanExplanation: FDA may withhold hearing when proffer raises no genuine and substantial factual issue.
entries.legalExplanation: Although the Court approved the summary-judgment system, the actual Hynson application required a hearing under its facts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 97
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Don't misstate that the manufacturer lost all hearing rights in the individual case.

entries.title: Board of Water, Light & Sinking Fund Commissioners v. FERC, 294 F.3d 1317 (11th Cir. 2002)
entries.summary: No evidentiary hearing was necessary when objections were policy disputes, not material fact disputes.
entries.laymanExplanation: No evidentiary hearing was necessary when objections were policy disputes, not material fact disputes.
entries.legalExplanation: Dictum suggested some factual disputes can be resolved adequately on written submissions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 97
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Compare record-only resolution versus oral confrontation.

topics.title: § 3.3 — Judicial Versus Institutional Decisionmaking (pp. 98–100)
topics.description: Classes 9–10 · competing administrative models; efficiency-versus-impartiality tradeoffs.

entries.title: Judicial model of administrative adjudication
entries.summary: Agency adjudication should resemble a court trial: independent and unbiased decider, meaningful adversarial procedures, evidence in record, and separation from investigative/prosecutorial staff.
entries.laymanExplanation: Treat the agency judge like a real judge, deciding fairly based on hearing evidence alone.
entries.legalExplanation: Prioritizes procedural fairness, perceived legitimacy, cross-examination and the exclusive record. Under strict model, no substantive off-record advice or contacts by parties and political figures.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 98–99
entries.examApplication: Use as normative justification for strict separation, neutral decisionmaker, and restrictions on secret communications.

entries.title: Institutional model of administrative adjudication
entries.summary: Agency is an integrated regulatory policymaking unit; staff collaborate and provide expertise and off-record advice to reach effective, consistent, and efficient decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Think of an agency as one expert team solving a regulatory problem.
entries.legalExplanation: Prioritizes specialized accuracy, effective implementation of public programs, and accountable regulatory policy rather than a courtroom boundary around every decision.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 98–99
entries.examApplication: Use to justify staff consultation, discretion, expertise, and agency-head policy control.

entries.title: Most administrative law is a compromise between the models
entries.summary: Actual systems mix safeguards and flexible internal agency teamwork, especially for final decision responsibility, ex parte contacts, legislative pressure, separation of functions, bias and judge independence.
entries.laymanExplanation: Neither complete courtroom rules nor total free-form teamwork prevails in every setting.
entries.legalExplanation: Determine which function is under examination, whether the case is Type A or B/C, whether adjudicative facts or policy are at issue, and which model's values control.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 99–100
entries.examTrap: The model labels are analytical frameworks, not independently binding legal tests.

topics.title: § 3.3.1 — Decisionmaker Responsibility (pp. 100–106)
topics.description: Classes 9–10 · Morgan I–IV, disclosure of proposals, record exclusivity, school teacher Rex assigned problem.

entries.title: Morgan I — 'the one who decides must hear'
entries.summary: The official responsible for final adjudication must personally consider and appraise the record and argument that justify the decision; it is permissible for examiners and staff to gather and summarize evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: The boss can use employees to gather evidence but cannot blindly sign their answer.
entries.legalExplanation: This is a statutory 'full hearing' principle articulated before the federal APA. It does not demand that the agency head attend every hearing or read every transcript page; decision must reflect conscientious consideration of evidentiary material.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 100–102
entries.rule: Final decisionmaker must consider and appraise evidence and argument underlying adjudicatory determination, not rubber-stamp an unseen case.
entries.examTrap: 'Must hear' is not literally 'must personally observe live witnesses'.

entries.title: Morgan v. United States (Morgan I), 298 U.S. 468 (1936)
entries.summary: No. The official who finally decides must meaningfully consider and appraise the evidentiary record and arguments, even if staff gathered or analyzed the evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: Simply: No. The official who finally decides must meaningfully consider and appraise the evidentiary record and arguments, even if staff gathered or analyzed the evidence.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Does a statutory 'full hearing' permit an official who has not considered the evidence or argument to issue the final administrative determination? Reasoning: A quasi-judicial hearing is not meaningful if the authorized decisionmaker is not guided by the evidentiary record. The agency is not an impersonal collective substitute for assigned decisionmaker responsibility; staff assistance remains permissible.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 100–102
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied reading
entries.facts: USDA stockyard-ratemaking proceedings were heard by an examiner; secretary ultimately approved rate order despite allegations he never reviewed evidence, briefs or argument. A separate acting secretary heard argument without receiving decision authority.
entries.issue: Does a statutory 'full hearing' permit an official who has not considered the evidence or argument to issue the final administrative determination?
entries.holding: No. The official who finally decides must meaningfully consider and appraise the evidentiary record and arguments, even if staff gathered or analyzed the evidence.
entries.reasoning: A quasi-judicial hearing is not meaningful if the authorized decisionmaker is not guided by the evidentiary record. The agency is not an impersonal collective substitute for assigned decisionmaker responsibility; staff assistance remains permissible.
entries.rule: A final administrative adjudicator cannot merely rubber-stamp a decision prepared without personal substantive record consideration.
entries.examApplication: Use when final agency head appears to have decided without record review; analyze alternatives to literal full-transcript reading.
entries.examTrap: Morgan I reached the adequacy of allegations at motion-to-dismiss stage, not a final finding that the USDA secretary failed to comply.

entries.title: Morgan v. United States (Morgan II), 304 U.S. 1 (1938)
entries.summary: Reading summaries, party briefs, and conferring with staff who reviewed evidence sufficiently complied with Morgan I.
entries.laymanExplanation: Reading summaries, party briefs, and conferring with staff who reviewed evidence sufficiently complied with Morgan I.
entries.legalExplanation: The same case also stressed fair notice of the government's proposed case and opportunity to meet it; proposed decisions are normally disclosed in APA proceedings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 102–104
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Do not assume personal review must equal independent original transcript reading.

entries.title: Practical ways to reconcile Morgan with modern agencies
entries.summary: Options include final adjudication by ALJ, discretionary agency-head review, delegation to a judicial officer, intermediate appellate boards, and agency head reliance on accurate summaries.
entries.laymanExplanation: A cabinet secretary can review important cases, delegate the rest, or rely on properly prepared summaries.
entries.legalExplanation: Each institutional design trades final policymaking control against workload and the judicial-model preference for an independently engaged adjudicator.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 102–103
entries.examApplication: Assess whether the authorized final decider actually considered sufficiently complete and accurate information.

entries.title: Proposed decisions, disclosure and objections
entries.summary: APA §§ 557(b), (c) generally require disclosure of proposed decisions and chance for exceptions before final agency action; outside APA, procedural due process and governing rules may impose narrower duties.
entries.laymanExplanation: The losing party often must see the hearing officer's findings before the final boss changes them.
entries.legalExplanation: Morgan II emphasized notice of the government's claims; Mackay Radio rejected automatic due process duty to issue proposed opinion without prejudice; Ballard highlights special-trial-judge report transparency under Tax Court rules.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 103–105
entries.examTrap: Do not overclaim that due process universally requires a written initial decision in every non-APA process.

entries.title: NLRB v. Mackay Radio & Telegraph Co., 304 U.S. 333 (1938)
entries.summary: Due process did not categorically require a proposed decision absent demonstrable prejudice.
entries.laymanExplanation: Due process did not categorically require a proposed decision absent demonstrable prejudice.
entries.legalExplanation: Book contrasts Morgan II's fairness concern with a narrower constitutional floor.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 103–104
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Mention prejudice when claimant lacked intermediate report.

entries.title: Ballard v. Commissioner, 544 U.S. 40 (2005)
entries.summary: Tax Court could not conceal special trial judge's report under its governing rules and avoid scrutiny of credibility findings.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax Court could not conceal special trial judge's report under its governing rules and avoid scrutiny of credibility findings.
entries.legalExplanation: Special trial judge observed witnesses; ultimate judge reversed credibility conclusions without disclosing the first report. Court stressed reporting transparency.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 104–105
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Distinguish interpretation of court rules from absolute constitutional requirement.

entries.title: Mazza v. Cavicchia, 105 A.2d 545 (N.J. 1954)
entries.summary: Undisclosed hearing-officer recommendations to license-revoking decisionmaker offended adjudicative fair play and exclusive-record norms.
entries.laymanExplanation: Undisclosed hearing-officer recommendations to license-revoking decisionmaker offended adjudicative fair play and exclusive-record norms.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook raises whether a confidential recommended decision is functionally like untested testimony.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 105
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Connect to Ballard and ex parte record concerns.

entries.title: United States v. Morgan (Morgan IV), 313 U.S. 409 (1941)
entries.summary: Judges normally cannot depose high-level adjudicators about internal decision mental processes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judges normally cannot depose high-level adjudicators about internal decision mental processes.
entries.legalExplanation: Morgan IV rejected intensive questioning of Secretary of Agriculture's private deliberations; protects judicial and administrative decisional integrity.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 105–106
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Combine presumption of regularity with exceptions requiring strong external indications.

entries.title: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe, 401 U.S. 402 (1971)
entries.summary: Only a strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior permits inquiry into administrative decisionmaker mental processes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Only a strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior permits inquiry into administrative decisionmaker mental processes.
entries.legalExplanation: A challenger cannot merely ask to depose the official to find out whether they truly read the file.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 106
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Distinguish legitimate record review from forbidden fishing expedition.

entries.title: Exclusive record and official-notice exception
entries.summary: Decisionmakers in record-based adjudication cannot rely on unadmitted factual evidence; official notice may be taken with an opportunity for rebuttal.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency cannot secretly rely on outside facts while pretending it decided only the hearing record.
entries.legalExplanation: APA § 556(e) makes transcript, exhibits, and filed papers the exclusive decisional record; relevant official-notice safeguards apply.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 105–106
entries.examApplication: Find whether a factual basis came from admitted materials, proper official notice, or impermissible outside communications.

topics.title: § 3.3.2 — Ex Parte Communications (pp. 106–116)
topics.description: Classes 9–10 · APA §§ 551(14), 557(d); PATCO; remedies; state law, White House and interest tests.

entries.title: Ex parte restrictions — formal APA adjudication
entries.summary: APA § 557(d) bars nonpublic merits-related communications between an interested person outside the agency and a decisional employee in an applicable formal adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: People with special stakes in a pending case should not privately lobby the judge about who should win.
entries.legalExplanation: § 551(14) defines ex parte contact as an off-public-record oral/written communication without reasonable prior notice; ordinary status requests are excepted, but disguised pressure can be merits-related.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 107–109
entries.elements: (1) Proceedings subject to § 557(d); (2) interested outside person; (3) agency adjudicative decider; (4) no prior notice/public record; (5) communication relevant to merits.
entries.examTrap: A status request may be permissible, but procedural labels do not immunize concealed merits pressure.

entries.title: Interested person, outside the agency, relevant to merits
entries.summary: Interested person need not be a named party: special stake beyond public's general interest suffices; merits relevance is construed broadly to include more than specific facts in issue.
entries.laymanExplanation: An industry leader can count as interested even without being a named litigant.
entries.legalExplanation: PATCO treats an outside union president as interested because of his distinctive stake in labor-policy and union consequences; status and procedural inquiries are generally exempt if genuinely non-merits-related.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 108–111
entries.examApplication: Apply interest threshold to outsider, government official, trade union, public member; separately ask whether content sought to affect pending adjudication.

entries.title: Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO) v. FLRA, 685 F.2d 547 (D.C. Cir. 1982)
entries.summary: Merits-related private attempts to influence adjudication are improper, but agency adjudication affected by such contacts is voidable rather than automatically void; on these facts the court did not vacate the decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: Simply: Merits-related private attempts to influence adjudication are improper, but agency adjudication affected by such contacts is voidable rather than automatically void; on these facts the court did not vacate the decision.
entries.legalExplanation: Issue: Were the off-record contacts forbidden under § 557(d) and, if so, must the resulting FLRA decision automatically be vacated? Reasoning: Lewis's ostensibly procedural contacts were close but did not prejudice PATCO because formal motion practice allowed opposition. Shanker's merits lobbying was plainly improper and Applewhaite should have stopped it, but no credible influence or party benefit justified vacatur.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 107–112
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in supplied reading
entries.facts: During formal FLRA adjudication over PATCO's illegal strike, Transportation Secretary Lewis privately pressed for prompt handling; labor leader Shanker dined with commissioner Applewhaite and urged leniency in pending union decertification.
entries.issue: Were the off-record contacts forbidden under § 557(d) and, if so, must the resulting FLRA decision automatically be vacated?
entries.holding: Merits-related private attempts to influence adjudication are improper, but agency adjudication affected by such contacts is voidable rather than automatically void; on these facts the court did not vacate the decision.
entries.reasoning: Lewis's ostensibly procedural contacts were close but did not prejudice PATCO because formal motion practice allowed opposition. Shanker's merits lobbying was plainly improper and Applewhaite should have stopped it, but no credible influence or party benefit justified vacatur.
entries.rule: Evaluate § 557(d) ex parte contacts and apply equitable taint/prejudice analysis; inappropriate contact alone does not necessarily require remand.
entries.examApplication: Classify each contact, then analyze seriousness, effect on decision, benefitting party, opportunity to respond, and value of a new hearing.
entries.examTrap: Shanker's misconduct was unmistakable; absence of vacatur is a remedies conclusion, not judicial approval.

entries.title: PATCO remedies and equitable vacatur factors
entries.summary: Agency remedies include public disclosure and, in appropriate cases, a show-cause requirement/adverse treatment of violating party; judicial courts consider whether irrevocable taint makes decision unfair.
entries.laymanExplanation: Improper secret lobbying should be exposed; overturning the decision depends on whether it actually compromised fairness.
entries.legalExplanation: Assess gravity; potential influence; whether violator benefited; non-disclosure and lost response opportunity; whether vacatur/remand would serve a purpose. Court retains equitable discretion, rather than mechanical automatic nullity.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 109–110
entries.elements: Gravity; possible influence; benefit; opposing party's opportunity to respond; utility of new proceedings.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse administrative disclosure and sanctions with automatic judicial invalidation.

entries.title: State MSAPA § 13 differs from federal APA § 557(d)
entries.summary: The 1961 MSAPA restricts communications on fact issues with any person/party and on law issues with a party/representative unless parties can participate, while permitting agency-member consultation and personal assistants.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some state rules use different categories of off-record communications than the federal test.
entries.legalExplanation: Compare protected subject matter (fact versus law), sender's identity, exceptions for other agency members and assistant advice, and the federal interested-person/merits standard.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 112–113
entries.examApplication: Choose law of the governing sovereign before applying PATCO.

entries.title: Johnson v. Department of the Air Force, 50 F.4th 110 (Fed. Cir. 2022)
entries.summary: Undisclosed off-record evidence to an employment hearing officer may violate constitutional due process even outside APA § 557(d).
entries.laymanExplanation: Undisclosed off-record evidence to an employment hearing officer may violate constitutional due process even outside APA § 557(d).
entries.legalExplanation: Supports a due-process backstop when a non-Type A decisionmaker receives new evidence not revealed to the employee.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 113
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Do not require Type A for every objection to unfair secret factual submissions.

entries.title: Idaho Historic Preservation Council v. City of Boise, 8 P.3d 646 (Idaho 2000)
entries.summary: Land-use appellate decision reversed after city council contacts with constituents were disclosed only generally, not as to content or speakers.
entries.laymanExplanation: Land-use appellate decision reversed after city council contacts with constituents were disclosed only generally, not as to content or speakers.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority found due process violation; dissent emphasized practical impossibility of cataloging every constituent contact with elected officials.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 113–115
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Contrast community politics and judicialized land-use decisions.

entries.title: Portland Audubon Society v. Endangered Species Committee, 984 F.2d 1534 (9th Cir. 1993)
entries.summary: President and White House aides were treated as outside interested persons for purposes of a formal adjudication's ex parte restrictions.
entries.laymanExplanation: President and White House aides were treated as outside interested persons for purposes of a formal adjudication's ex parte restrictions.
entries.legalExplanation: God Squad decided ESA timber-habitat exception; statute vested decisional authority in Committee, not President. Compare executive role in ordinary rulemaking.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 114–115
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in textbook notes (not reproduced opinion)
entries.examApplication: Contrast Sierra Club v. Costle's allowance of presidential involvement in rulemaking.

entries.title: Internal versus external ex parte contacts
entries.summary: § 3.3.2 focuses on outsiders lobbying adjudicators; § 3.3.4 concerns internal agency advisers and whether they previously served investigative/prosecutorial roles.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency official talking to outsiders raises different rules from speaking with agency colleagues.
entries.legalExplanation: Determine if communicator is outside agency or inside; for internal contacts ask whether staff served as advocate in same or factually related case and whether separation-of-functions rules apply.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 3, pp. 106–107, 115
entries.examTrap: An authorized internal policy adviser is not automatically an improper § 557(d) external interested person.
